title: Deborah under the palm tree (Judges 4:4–5)
hookLine: a prophetess judges Israel from beneath her own palm tree
tomorrow: I will surely go with thee (Judges 4:6–10)

lines: A PALM TREE WITH A NAME.
A WOMAN UNDER THE TREE, LISTENING.
cards: Between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, there's a palm tree with a name.
People walk up the road to it, carrying, one can only guess, the usual things: a boundary stone that moved, a debt, a quarrel between neighbors. Under the tree sits a woman. The times are hard.
After Ehud, the dial of Judges has turned again, and a Canaanite king named Jabin has pressed Israel hard, with a captain called Sisera and his chariots of iron.
And in the middle of all that, the book stops to show us a woman under a tree, listening.

teach.h: A PROPHETESS, A WIFE, A JUDGE.
teach.b: Here's how the text introduces her: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." Three things in one breath: a prophetess, married, and a judge. Remember the word shofet?
Ehud was a rescuer with a blade. Deborah is a judge in the sense the word sounds like. She hears cases.

teach.h: THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL CAME UP TO HER.
teach.b: The next verse says where: under the palm tree of Deborah, "and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment." She doesn't travel the country or summon anyone, not yet. People come up to her.
Tradition has asked about the details.
A teaching in the Talmud links the name Lapidoth to torches, and says she made wicks for the lamps of the sanctuary.

The same teaching asks why a palm tree, and suggests she judged in the open air, where anyone could see, rather than alone behind a closed door. The Talmud also counts her among seven women it calls prophetesses.
The text itself stays short: two verses, and the story moves on.
But they describe a different kind of leadership from Ehud's: no army, no hidden blade, just a place people know to go when they need someone wise and willing to listen.
In a book full of cycles and crises, a tree where people bring their quarrels is its own kind of rescue.

how: Jews read Deborah's story in Judges 4 and 5, and the Talmud discusses her among the women it calls prophetesses; the chapters are also read in synagogue as a haftarah.

o: a judge: here, one who hears the people's cases
a palm tree where the tribes gathered for war
a prophetess who speaks God's word to kings

s: Deborah traveled around Israel hearing cases
the people came up to her, under the palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim.
the Talmud counts Deborah among the prophetesses
it names her among seven women it calls prophetesses.
Deborah's introduction calls her a prophetess and a judge
and the wife of Lapidoth, all in one verse.

games.q: you're Deborah. people are coming up the road with their quarrels. where do you hear them?
o: inside a house, with the door shut.
out in the open, under the palm tree.
you send them away until the war is over.
games.why: she judges under the palm tree of Deborah, and a teaching in the Talmud says the open air was the point: anyone could see.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has brought you a problem lately, or might soon: a friend, a colleague, a child, a parent.

Before any advice, picture just listening, the way people walked up the road to Deborah and found her already there, and ask what they'd need to say first. If no one comes to mind, think of who you would walk up the road to.

wordCard.voice: shofet. The word for judge that fits Deborah, a prophetess who judged Israel in the hill country of Ephraim, where the people came up to her for judgment. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: judging, said of a woman: the feminine of shofet, used for Deborah in Judges 4:4.

carryVoice: Your line: deborah judged. People came up to her, and she listened. See you tomorrow.
